title: Duplication
description: The duplication exclusion, IRC § 41(d)(4)(C), bars claims for reproducing an existing business component from examination, plans or public information.
summary: The duplication exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) bars U.S. taxpayers from claiming the federal R&D tax credit for reproducing an existing business component, in whole or in part, from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information. Merely examining a competitor's product while independently developing your own component through experimentation does not trigger the exclusion.

body.text: The duplication exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) bars U.S. taxpayers from claiming the federal R&D tax credit for reproducing an existing business component, in whole or in part, from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information. Merely examining a competitor's product while independently developing your own component through experimentation does not trigger the exclusion.

The duplication exclusion codified at Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41(d)(4)(C) and interpreted by Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.41-4(c)(4) bars taxpayers from claiming the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit for activities related to reproducing an existing business component—in whole or in part—from a physical examination of the component itself, or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information. Enacted originally in 1981 (Pub. L. 97–34, title II, § 221, Aug. 13, 1981, 95 Stat. 241, effective for amounts paid or incurred after June 30, 1981, originally codified at IRC § 44F, renumbered § 41 by Pub. L. 99–514 on Oct. 22, 1986, and made permanent by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015) to encourage business firms to perform technological research that increases the innovative qualities and operational efficiency of the U.S. economy, Section 41 draws a strict statutory boundary between experimental development and the replication of established designs. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4)—promulgated in final form by Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9104 effective January 2, 2004, for expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, and currently in force as of November 2026—merely examining an existing component in the course of developing a taxpayer's own component does not trigger disqualification; rather, the exclusion applies when physical inspection, client drawings, or public technical data substitute for resolving technical uncertainty through a systematic process of experimentation.

For corporate taxpayers and tax practitioners preparing IRS Form 6765 (which incorporates Section G—Business Component Information on an optional basis for tax years beginning before 2026 and on a mandatory basis for tax years beginning after 2025 under the December 2025 and June 2026 revised instructions), managing duplication exposure demands component-level discipline from project inception. Because the 80% "substantially all" rule of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) applies separately to each discrete business component, allowing excluded duplication or reverse-engineering activities to exceed 20% of research effort disqualifies the entire business component unless the taxpayer retains granular subcomponent records sufficient to invoke the "shrinking-back" rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)—an evidentiary burden underscored by the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and the Tax Court in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113. Furthermore, even when experimental activities satisfy the 80% or greater threshold, any remaining 20% or lesser activities that constitute excluded duplication under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) remain ineligible for inclusion in QREs under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6).
Statutory, Regulatory, and Policy Foundations of the Duplication Exclusion
Policy Purpose and Economic Framing

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-1(a), Section 41 is designed to encourage businesses to undertake the technological research needed to expand the innovative qualities and operational efficiency of the U.S. economy, making the credit available whether a qualifying research project ultimately succeeds or fails.

GAO-10-136 further establishes that a well-targeted statutory definition of QREs—and rigorous IRS enforcement of statutory exclusions—improves the economic efficiency of the credit by directing tax subsidies toward research with high external benefits and away from activities with low external benefits. However, direct examination of the accessible text of GAO-10-136 demonstrates that the GAO report itself does not explicitly use the terms "appropriability problem", "knowledge spillovers", or "reverse engineering". Rather, the explicit attribution of knowledge spillovers to competitor reverse engineering is documented in U.S. Department of the Treasury Office of Tax Analysis guidance (Research and Experimentation (R&E) Credit, October 12, 2016) and Congressional Research Service (CRS) Report RL31181 (Federal Research Tax Credit: Current Law and Policy Issues), which explain that innovating firms cannot capture all returns on R&D because once an idea is developed, returns spill over to competitors through reverse engineering, migration of research scientists and engineers, and diffusion of general technical knowledge. Subsidizing the party that merely copies or reverse-engineers an innovation would therefore subsidize the free-rider channel itself rather than the creation of positive knowledge spillovers.
Statutory Prohibition: IRC Section 41(d)(4)(C)

Section 41(d)(4) of Title 26 enumerates specific activities categorically excluded from "qualified research" regardless of whether they might otherwise appear to involve engineering effort. Under the statutory heading "Duplication of existing business component" in IRC § 41(d)(4)(C), no credit is permitted for any research related to reproducing an existing business component—in whole or in part—from any of three specified informational channels:

items: Physical examination of the business component itself (such as physical teardowns, dimensional metrology, disassembly, or chemical composition testing);
Technical design documentation, specifically plans, blueprints, or detailed specifications; or

Publicly available information with respect to the business component (such as published patents, technical manuals, academic literature, or industry specifications sufficiently detailed to enable replication).

body.text: From an audit and cost-accounting standpoint, because the statute disqualifies activities relating to reproduction "in whole or in part", any employee wages (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)), tangible supplies (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)), off-premises computer rental costs (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)), or third-party contract research outlays (IRC § 41(b)(3)) allocable to copying an existing item through these channels must be excluded from QREs.
Regulatory Safe Harbor: 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(4) and Separate Business Components

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(4)—adopted in T.D. 9104, effective January 2, 2004, for expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, and currently in force—tracks the statutory bar while adding an essential safe-harbor sentence that protects legitimate competitive research:

"(4) Duplication of existing business component. Activities relating to reproducing an existing business component (in whole or in part) from a physical examination of the business component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information about the business component are not qualified research. This exclusion does not apply merely because the taxpayer examines an existing business component in the course of developing its own business component."

As corroborated by the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 — Qualified Research Activities (June 2005), evaluating another party's business component during the course of developing a taxpayer's own business component does not by itself trigger the duplication exclusion.

Equally critical to applying the exclusion accurately is the statutory scope of a "business component" under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B), defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b), the qualification tests of Section 41 must be applied separately to each discrete business component of the taxpayer. Consequently, product development and manufacturing-process development are analyzed independently: if a manufacturer reproduces an existing chemical molecule or standard mechanical part (which is excluded at the product level under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C)), its concurrent experimental efforts to develop a novel, technically uncertain synthesis route, specialized production mold/tooling, or automated assembly process constitute a separate process business component eligible for evaluation on its own technical merits.
Duplication (IRC Section 41(d)(4)(C)) Versus Funded Research (IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H))

cells: IRC Citation
Treasury Regulation
Excluded Activity
Activities relating to reproducing an existing business component (in whole or in part) from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information
Any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity
Operative Legal Test
Whether existing plans, physical teardowns, or public technical data dictated the replicated design instead of independent experimentation to resolve technical uncertainty
Whether payment to the researcher is contingent on the success of the research (financial risk) AND the researcher retains substantial rights in the research results
Core Policy Function
Preventing federal tax subsidies for copying or reverse-engineering existing technologies that add no new technical capability
Allocating R&D credit eligibility between contracting parties and preventing dual claims on third-party commissioned research

body.text: Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(2), all agreements entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons are evaluated to determine the extent of funding. If a taxpayer performs research on behalf of another person and retains no substantial rights in the research under the governing agreement (for example, where the agreement confers on the client the exclusive right to exploit the results of the research, as incidental benefits like increased experience do not constitute substantial rights), the research is treated as fully funded, and no expenses paid or incurred by the performing contractor qualify as QREs—regardless of whether the contract is fixed-price. Moreover, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2), if a researcher retains no substantial rights in the research and the payments to the researcher are contingent upon the success of the research (meaning the payor does not bear the expense if the research is unsuccessful), neither the performer nor the person paying for the research is entitled to treat any portion of the expenditures as QREs. Conversely, if a researcher retains substantial rights under the agreement, the research is treated as funded to the extent of the non-contingent payments received, requiring the researcher to reduce otherwise qualified expenses by the funding received (subject to a pro rata allocation rule under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(3), under which in no event may less than 65% of the funding be applied against otherwise qualified research expenses). In third-party manufacturing or engineering arrangements, a contractor must therefore satisfy both statutory exclusions independently: it must bear financial risk and retain substantial rights under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d), and its engineering activities must resolve technical uncertainty rather than merely reproducing client-supplied blueprints under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4).
Interaction Between Duplication and the IRC Section 41(d)(1) Four-Part Test

Even apart from the explicit categorical exclusions in IRC § 41(d)(4), any claimed research activity must affirmatively satisfy every element of the foundational Four-Part Test codified at IRC § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2). Activities constituting duplication under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) simultaneously fail multiple prongs of IRC § 41(d)(1).
The Section 174 Threshold Test (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A))

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i), research expenditures must qualify as expenditures which may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174 (or, following the enactment of Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A and foreign research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174, though foreign research remains excluded from Section 41 under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)). Under 26 CFR §§ 1.174-1 and 1.174-2, research and experimental expenditures are defined as expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business which represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense". As U.S. Tax Court jurisprudence emphasizes (citing Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, and Stephens v. Commissioner), Section 174 as a general rule applies to the costs of developing the concept of a product rather than the costs of building the product itself—unless constructing a physical pilot model is necessary to evaluate and resolve technical uncertainty concerning the viability of the concept. Because copying a known design from physical measurements, teardown inspections, or client blueprints executes an established fabrication path rather than laboratory-sense concept experimentation, pure duplication fails the Section 174 threshold test at the outset.
The Discovering Technological Information and Uncertainty Test (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B))

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(ii) and (a)(4), qualified research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature—meaning the process of experimentation used to discover such information must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science—and the application of which is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information only if it is undertaken to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component.

Although 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) (promulgated in T.D. 9104 effective January 2, 2004) confirms that a taxpayer is not required to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering, duplication fails even this taxpayer-specific uncertainty threshold. When a company possesses detailed blueprints, engineering specifications, or physical teardown measurements of the target item, the information available to that taxpayer already establishes the capability, method, and appropriate design of the replicated component.
The Process of Experimentation Test (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(a)(5))

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. The governing regulation mandates three core procedural elements:

items: The taxpayer must identify the uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component that is the object of the taxpayer's research activities;
The taxpayer must identify one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty; and
The taxpayer must identify and conduct a process of evaluating the alternatives—through, for example, modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology—to resolve the uncertainty.

body.text: Furthermore, under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), this evaluative process must be conducted for a "qualified purpose"—specifically, a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component—and IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) expressly disqualifies any research related to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Crucially, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) cautions that a process of experimentation must be an evaluative process and generally should be capable of evaluating more than one alternative; the mere existence of uncertainty regarding the appropriate design does not by itself convert all development work into a process of experimentation. Duplication inherently pursues a single predetermined replicative target rather than formulating hypotheses and evaluating competing technical alternatives, leaving only quality-control verification (excluded under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(7)) to confirm that the copy matches the original.
The 80% Substantially All Rule and the Residual Exclusion Trap (26 CFR Section 1.41-4(a)(6))

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), "substantially all" of the research activities with respect to each discrete business component—defined strictly as 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (such as employee hours)—must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. As articulated by the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the "substantially all" fraction is calculated by dividing (a) the research activities that constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose by (b) all research activities with respect to that business component that are not excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4) and are deductible under Section 174.

Reading 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) in full reveals a two-part compliance hazard whenever reverse engineering or duplication is commingled with genuine experimentation inside a single project. Second, even if independent experimentation reaches 85% of activities and excluded duplication accounts for 15%, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) permits the remaining 20% or lesser non-experimental research activities to qualify only "so long as these remaining research activities satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1)(A) and are not otherwise excluded under section 41(d)(4)". Because duplication is categorically excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C), that 15% duplicative share cannot "ride along" inside the 20% residual buffer of the substantially-all rule and must still be carved out of claimed QREs.
Reverse Engineering, Trade Secret Law Parallels, and the Plans and Blueprints Trap
Reverse Engineering as Baseline Evaluation Versus Disqualified Replication

In general engineering and commercial usage, "reverse engineering" describes the process of analyzing a physical system, chemical compound, or software program to identify its subcomponents and functional relationships. Under IRC § 41, however, reverse engineering is tightly circumscribed. In its Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software, the IRS explicitly instructs examiners that reverse-engineering activities—such as examining existing programs, databases, and files, or reverse-engineering legacy code to determine all requirements and processing algorithms that a rewritten application must support—are not qualified research under IRC § 41(d), citing 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8.

In 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8, Taxpayer X analyzes and reproduces ingredients A and B contained in Competitor Y's commercial additive, where the differences between the ingredients in Y's additive and those reproduced by X are insignificant and immaterial to the viability, effectiveness, or cost of the additive. Concurrently, Taxpayer X wishes to replace ingredient C of Competitor Y's additive with an alternative ingredient of materially lower cost, and engages in a systematic process of experimentation to develop, analyze, and test potential alternative formulations to replace ingredient C. The Treasury Regulation concludes that Taxpayer X's activities in analyzing and reproducing ingredients A and B constitute the duplication of existing business components and are excluded from qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4), whereas Taxpayer X's experimental activities to develop and test alternative formulations to replace ingredient C do not involve duplication and are not excluded under paragraph (c)(4). Reading 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8 together with the safe harbor in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) establishes a clear analytical demarcation between permissible competitive benchmarking and disqualified replication:

headers: Qualified Competitive Development (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) Safe Harbor)

cells: Purpose of Inspection
Benchmarking performance metrics, identifying competitor limitations, or establishing functional targets to inform an independent design
Extracting exact physical dimensions, alloy/chemical compositions (e.g., ingredients A and B in Example 8), source code, or legacy interface logic to replicate them
Technical Uncertainty
Information available to the taxpayer still leaves capability, method, or appropriate design uncertain (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i))
Teardown measurements, reverse-engineered code, or client specifications dictate the design, leaving only conformance verification
Development Process
Formulating hypotheses and systematically evaluating competing design alternatives (e.g., replacing ingredient C in Example 8) (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i))
Direct dimensional copying, specification translation, COBOL-to-C++ code conversion, or build-to-print fabrication
Output Component
Independently engineered product, subcomponent, formulation, or novel manufacturing process (IRC § 41(d)(2)(B))
Reproduced business component (in whole or in part) derived from physical examination, blueprints, or public data

body.text: Trade Secret Law Parallels: 18 U.S.C. Section 1839 and Readily Ascertainable Information

Under 18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)(B), the definition of "improper means" in trade secret misappropriation expressly "does not include reverse engineering, independent derivation, or any other lawful means of acquisition". Correspondingly, 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(B) defines scientific, technical, or engineering information as a protected "trade secret" only if "the information derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable through proper means by, another person who can obtain economic value from the disclosure or use of the information".

Analytically, however, tax practitioners must carefully distinguish the DTSA's objective "readily ascertainable" standard from the subjective, taxpayer-specific uncertainty standard under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3). In trade secret litigation under 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(B), if a product's design is readily ascertainable through proper inspection of a marketed unit, the design loses trade secret protection as an objective matter. By contrast, because 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)–(ii) evaluates whether the information available to the taxpayer establishes the capability, method, or appropriate design—and does not require the taxpayer to seek information exceeding the common knowledge of skilled professionals—the mere commercial availability of a rival product in the marketplace does not bar an R&D tax credit when a taxpayer chooses independent derivation through systematic experimentation. Conversely, when a taxpayer actually acquires a commercial unit and extracts a readily ascertainable design through physical teardown and dimensional measurement, that physical examination simultaneously supplies the design information to the taxpayer (eliminating uncertainty under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)) and triggers the express statutory bar on reproduction from a physical examination of the business component under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C).
The Plans, Blueprints, and Detailed Specifications Trap

IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) explicitly exclude reproduction from "plans, blueprints, detailed specifications", creating acute audit exposure for contract manufacturers, aerospace and automotive suppliers, and "build-to-print" fabricators.

When a client furnishes a detailed computer-aided design (CAD) model or blueprint specifying exact part geometry, dimensional tolerances, and material grades, fabricating the product reproduces the client's detailed specification and is barred at the product-design level under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4). In that build-to-print posture, the manufacturer's primary statutory pathway—assuming the work satisfies the unfunded research rules of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(3), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)—is to isolate and claim a separate, technically uncertain manufacturing process, die/mold tooling, or assembly technique as a distinct business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b). By contrast, when a client provides only functional performance specifications (for example, requiring a valve assembly that can withstand a specified pressure and temperature envelope within a maximum weight limit, or submitting a request for quote with general product parameters as in TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009)) without supplying a design blueprint, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) permits a process of experimentation because the "appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities", avoiding the blueprint duplication exclusion.
Judicial Precedents Governing Duplication, Subcomponents, and Routine Engineering
Federal courts adjudicate duplication concepts in close conjunction with the process-of-experimentation, business-component, supply-eligibility, and substantiation rules.
Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201 (Oct. 1, 2014): Independent Development of Competing Products

In Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201 (filed October 1, 2014), Estech Systems, Inc. (ESI), an S corporation founded by CEO and product visionary Eric Suder that designed and manufactured business telephone and voicemail systems, claimed Section 41 research credits for tax years 2004 through 2007 across 76 projects, 12 of which were stipulated by the parties as a representative trial sample. During the three-week trial (which generated over 3,500 pages of testimony and 170,000 pages of exhibits), the IRS and its expert witness, Dr. Jackson, argued that ESI's hardware and software projects were routine engineering and impermissible duplications—specifically asserting in Dr. Jackson's report that ESI "created products that merely matched products already available from other vendors" and that "ESI's strength is building low-cost, easy-to-use telephone systems that match products introduced earlier by industry leaders such as Avaya and Cisco".

The Tax Court rejected Dr. Jackson's expert report as unreliable and upheld R&D credit qualification for the sampled projects. The Court noted that Dr. Jackson offered no factual basis for his duplication assertions: Dr. Jackson did not compare a single circuit board designed by Avaya or Cisco to a circuit board designed by ESI's hardware engineers, nor did he compare a single line of software code written by Avaya or Cisco to code written by ESI's software engineers, and he admitted classifying projects as routine or nonroutine based merely on his general knowledge of the English language. Credible testimony from ESI's Senior Vice President of Product Development, Mr. Wende, and engineering witness Mr. Hoth established that ESI followed a systematic, four-stage product development process (Concept to Hardware to Software to Testing) to resolve genuine hardware and software uncertainties—such as modifying open-source Linux code that could not run straight from the internet on ESI's proprietary hardware (the Mad Max project), overcoming severe acoustic noise and current spike challenges when adding analog phone lines to a compact chassis (the DLC82 project), and integrating 3.3-volt surface-mounted parts, a ColdFire processor, and 20 MHz digital signal processors (the IVC1212 project).
"Neither section 41 nor the regulations thereunder require taxpayers to 'reinvent the wheel.'"

Suder thus stands as the leading Tax Court precedent confirming that developing a commercial product that competes with or matches the high-level market features of industry leaders like Avaya and Cisco is not excluded duplication under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) or 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) when the taxpayer lacks access to the competitors' proprietary circuit boards, blueprints, or source code and instead resolves design and method uncertainties through its own systematic process of experimentation.
TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (Nov. 12, 2009): Supply QREs for Production Tooling

In TG Missouri, an automotive injection-molding manufacturer received customer requests for quotes containing general product specifications, entered into contracts to develop specialized production molds, and either constructed the molds in-house or contracted with third-party toolmakers—retaining and depreciating some molds while purchasing other finished molds from third parties and reselling them to its automotive customers. The legal issue decided by the Tax Court at 133 T.C. 278 was whether the costs paid to third parties for production molds that TG Missouri resold to its customers were excluded from QRE "supplies" under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and IRC § 174(c) as "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation". Ruling in favor of the taxpayer (133 T.C. at 297), the Tax Court held that production molds held for resale to customers were not depreciable property in TG Missouri's hands and therefore properly qualified as supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)—a precedent subsequently cited by the Tax Court in Stephens v. Commissioner to confirm that a contractual obligation to build and deliver a product to a customer does not preclude the taxpayer from resolving technical uncertainty while developing that item. Accordingly, while isolating production tooling or molding processes from customer-designed parts is a valid compliance strategy grounded directly in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b), TG Missouri itself governs the depreciable-property exclusion for supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) rather than the duplication exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C).
Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. Mar. 7, 2023): Activity Dilution and Shrinking-Back Proof

In Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, affirmed, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. March 7, 2023, No. 21-3145), taxpayer's shipbuilding subsidiary Corn Island Shipyard, Inc. (CIS) claimed Section 41 credits for the tax year ending June 2014 across 11 "first-in-class" marine vessels, stipulating to try two representative vessels as pilot models: the Apex 720 Tanker (Project 720, for which CIS claimed $2,505,491 in production wages and $3,892,142 in supply costs) and the Detyens Dry Dock (Project 730, for which CIS claimed $146,109 in production wages and $1,943,265 in supply costs), alongside $609,276 in unallocated nonproduction employee wages across all 11 vessels.

Both the Tax Court and the Seventh Circuit nonetheless disallowed 100% of the claimed research credit on three doctrinal grounds that directly govern duplication and prior-design adaptation. First, regarding novelty versus research activities in the 80% substantially-all fraction, the Seventh Circuit held that showing 87% of production hours were tied to items differing from the predecessor Penn 80—or that the Detyens Dry Dock was the first dry dock CIS had ever built—did not satisfy the 80% "substantially all" rule of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), because the statutory fraction measures research activities constituting elements of a process of experimentation, not physical component novelty relative to a prior model; much of the engineering design spiral addressed generic manufacturing uncertainty rather than investigative design uncertainty. Second, post-fabrication testing—specifically the deadweight survey measuring water displacement on the Apex 720 Tanker and the partial raise-and-lower test on the Detyens Dry Dock (where the customer conducted the full raise-and-lower test after delivery)—constituted quality-control testing under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(7) to confirm whether customer contract specifications were met, rather than a methodical plan to test a scientific hypothesis, analyze data, refine the hypothesis, and retest. Third, although the Seventh Circuit recognized that iterative engineering work on specific novel subcomponents (such as the Tanker's redesigned stern notch, towing bridle, or the Dry Dock's outboard side plate) might have involved a qualifying process of experimentation if isolated, CIS pursued an "all or nothing" trial strategy claiming each vessel in its entirety and relied on arbitrary percentage estimates without maintaining subcomponent-level cost or time records; because the court had no evidentiary basis to apportion wages or supplies to discrete subcomponents, the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) could not rescue any portion of the credit.
Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Dec. 23, 2024): Routine Engineering and Public Codes

While the Tax Court entered an interlocutory discovery order in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 4759-22, on August 29, 2023 (denying a motion for a protective order regarding sampled projects), the merits trial opinion disallowing the claimed R&D credits and upholding accuracy-related penalties was issued on December 23, 2024, in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113.

In Phoenix Design Group—involving research credits generated in tax years 2013 ($138,205), 2014 ($158,031), 2015 ($138,334), and 2016 ($128,228) and claimed/applied across examination credit years 2015 ($110,576), 2016 ($74,488), 2017 ($211,142), 2018 ($68,147), and 2019 ($71,102)—a Tennessee consulting engineering firm (PDG) claimed wage QREs across three sampled construction projects for designing mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF, including HVAC) building systems for hospitals and medical facilities. Judge Greaves held that none of the three sampled projects entailed qualified research under IRC § 41 and sustained accuracy-related penalties.

Specifically, PDG argued that it faced objective uncertainty regarding the design of complete hospital MEPF systems because its engineers initially did not know the building footprint. Judge Greaves rejected this contention, finding that at the outset of projects such as BHNM Oxford, project architects furnished schematic block diagrams and preliminary master plans detailing floor layouts, department locations, and building configurations; for PDG's experienced senior hospital engineers, these preliminary architectural plans resolved general system design uncertainty. Furthermore, where PDG argued that adapting designs to published building codes, hybrid operating rooms, or equipment requirements created qualifying uncertainty, the Tax Court held that PDG's engineers merely applied their standard professional training and expertise to make design choices, perform routine preliminary calculations, and comply with standard building codes—falling short of a scientific-method process of experimentation. Finally, when the Court attempted to apply the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) to discrete technical issues, the effort failed because PDG's timesheets recorded only generic discipline labels (such as John Wade billing to "HVAC", Joseph Barnes to "ltg, pwr, sys design", and Richard Miller to "work on plumbing fixtures") and its unexplained final design drawings illustrated only final engineering solutions rather than any experimental evaluation of alternatives. Analytically, Phoenix Design Group reinforces the Tax Court's earlier decision in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37 (decided April 15, 2019, disallowing credits for tax years ended May 31, 2011 and May 31, 2012), confirming that applying established engineering formulas, client schematic plans, and publicly available building codes (IRC § 41(d)(4)(C)) without documented hypothesis testing fails the Four-Part Test.
Industry-Specific Applications of the Duplication Exclusion
Software Development: Legacy Porting, Interface Reverse Engineering, and Internal Use Software

Software R&D claims encounter rigorous duplication and adaptation scrutiny across four recurring examination scenarios documented in the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software and the Treasury Regulations.

First, in the IRS Software Audit Guidelines, moving an application to a new hardware platform (e.g., migrating from mainframe to PC) or a new software operating system (e.g., migrating from Windows to UNIX) is classified as re-hosting or porting. However, when a taxpayer rewrites an existing application in a new programming language—such as rewriting a legacy COBOL mainframe application into C++ or Java—the IRS Software Audit Guidelines explicitly state that such rewrites generally involve reverse engineering the existing code to determine all functional requirements and processing algorithms that the rewritten software must support, converting original code constructs into the new language without a new application architecture or process of experimentation. Using legacy source code as a complete functional specification therefore implicates both adaptation (IRC § 41(d)(4)(B)) and duplication/reverse engineering (IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8), unless the taxpayer is migrating to a fundamentally different computing architecture (such as refactoring a monolithic batch mainframe system into a distributed, real-time cloud microservices architecture) where legacy algorithms cannot establish the appropriate design.

Second, the IRS Software Audit Guidelines specify that reverse-engineering existing programs, databases, and files to determine how an existing application works, or writing software to use documented hardware device interfaces (such as disks, scanners, printers, or modems) and publicly available vendor Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), is not qualified research. Following a vendor's published API manual applies publicly available specifications (IRC § 41(d)(4)(C)) and routine debugging unless the integration confronts genuine architectural uncertainty (such as overcoming undocumented high-concurrency throughput limits through experimental data-streaming protocols).

Third, when a taxpayer develops software that is "substantially similar in technology, functionality, and features to capabilities already in existence at other companies" by examining rival user-interface screens and feature sets, the IRS Software Audit Guidelines instruct examiners to scrutinize whether existing marketplace technologies and computer-science methods already established how to build the software, requiring the taxpayer to substantiate independent architectural experimentation as in Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201.

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(i)–(iii) and (vi), software is developed primarily for internal use if it is developed for general and administrative (G&A) functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business—specifically limited to financial management functions, human resources management functions, and support services functions. Unless exempted (such as software developed for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research, software used in a production process meeting IRC § 41(d)(1), or a new or improved package of software and hardware developed together as a single product), internal-use software (and the internal subset of dual-function software where the 25% safe harbor does not apply) must satisfy the three-part High Threshold of Innovation Test under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi):

items: Innovative: The software must be intended to result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed that is substantial and economically significant;

Significant Economic Risk: The taxpayer must commit substantial resources to the development and there must be substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period; and

Commercial Availability: The software must not be commercially available for use by the taxpayer without modifications that are themselves of a nature that satisfies the innovation and significant economic risk requirements.

body.text: Crucially, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6), Example 8 does not address HR software customization; rather, as documented in the October 4, 2016 Federal Register rulemaking, Example 8 analyzes third-party interaction under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B) (evaluating whether software that enables third parties to initiate functions or upload and modify photographs online on the taxpayer's system is developed to interact with third parties and thus excepted from IUS treatment). Conversely, the regulatory "Example 8" that actually governs duplication and reverse engineering is 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8 (the competitor additive example), as cited in both the IRS General R&D Audit Techniques Guide and the IRS Software Audit Guidelines.
Manufacturing (Build-to-Print Operations)

In contract and discrete manufacturing, when an Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) supplies a detailed engineering drawing or CAD file of a mechanical bracket, housing, or component, fabricating that part reproduces the OEM's detailed specification and is excluded at the product level under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4). However, under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) and the IRS General R&D Audit Techniques Guide, a build-to-print vendor can legitimately claim Section 41 QREs by defining its manufacturing process, progressive die/mold tooling, or automated assembly technique—such as experimenting with multi-zone cooling rates, gating geometries, and mold-flow simulations to prevent thin-wall alloy warping—as the discrete business component, provided that the manufacturing process itself confronted genuine technical uncertainty (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)) and the contract was not funded within the meaning of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d).
Pharmaceuticals: Generic Drugs (ANDA) Versus Process and Formulation R&D

Reproducing an off-patent brand-name (innovator) drug molecule to demonstrate bioequivalence implicates IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) at the active-compound level because the active chemical structure and reference parameters are publicly available.

Instead, current IRS examination policy governing generic and Over-the-Counter (OTC) pharmaceuticals is established in IRS Publication 5931 (Audit Technique Guide — Pharmaceutical Industry Research Credit, revised April 1, 2024).

As documented in IRS Publication 5931, generic drugs are approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) through the Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA) process—termed "abbreviated" because the applicant is generally not required to conduct animal experiments or human clinical trials to establish safety and efficacy. Instead, an ANDA applicant must demonstrate that the generic drug has the same active ingredient (though inactive excipients need not be identical), performs the same, and is bioequivalent to an already FDA-approved innovator drug in dosage form, strength, route of administration, quality, performance characteristics, and intended use. Similarly, OTC drugs are brought to market either through the NDA/ANDA application process or the OTC Drug Review Monograph process. Publication 5931 explicitly instructs IRS examiners that both generic and OTC drugs utilizing an ANDA submission are higher-risk audit areas requiring additional examination review compared to NDA or Biologics License Application (BLA) products, that drug manufacturers must substantiate that research activities performed during drug development do not constitute excluded activities under IRC § 41(d)(4) (including the duplication exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(C)), and that FDA application user fees paid under the Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) or Medical Drug User Fee Amendment (MDUFA) must be excluded from QRE submissions.

Consistent with IRC § 41(d)(2)(B), T.D. 9104 (26 CFR § 1.41-4), and IRS Publication 5931, generic and specialty pharmaceutical companies can avoid active-molecule duplication by isolating a separate, non-duplicated business component: either Process R&D (developing a novel, technically uncertain chemical synthesis pathway to manufacture the active pharmaceutical ingredient at higher purity or yield) or Formulation and Delivery R&D (developing a new dosage or delivery form—such as converting an immediate-release formulation into an extended-release delivery system—that requires FDA approval and experimental testing of inactive excipient alternatives).
IRS Examination Scrutiny and the Shrinking-Back Defense
Baseline-Versus-Outcome Audit Scrutiny

Substantively, however, the official IRS Software Audit Guidelines and General R&D Audit Techniques Guide do instruct examiners reviewing "substantially similar" marketplace products or modified existing designs to issue Information Document Requests (IDRs) and conduct technical interviews evaluating whether available market technologies, vendor specifications, or legacy codebases already established the appropriate design at the outset of the project, or whether the taxpayer genuinely confronted beginning-of-project technical uncertainty requiring a systematic process of experimentation (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3) and (a)(5)).
The Shrinking-Back Rule Defense (26 CFR Section 1.41-4(b)(2))

When a complex product or system incorporates duplicated, standard, or adapted elements alongside genuinely novel engineering, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)—officially titled the "Shrinking-back rule"—provides the governing regulatory defense:

"(2) Shrinking-back rule. The requirements of section 41(d) and paragraph (a) of this section are to be applied first at the level of the discrete business component, that is, the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. If these requirements are not met at that level, then they apply at the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license. This shrinking back of the product is to continue until either a subset of elements of the product that satisfies the requirements is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and such element fails to satisfy the test. This shrinking-back rule is applied only if a taxpayer does not satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1) and paragraph (a)(2) of this section with respect to the overall business component. The shrinking-back rule is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility."

Immediately following the rule, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(3) sets forth the official regulatory illustration (the Carburetor Example): Taxpayer X, a motorcycle engine builder, develops a new carburetor for use in a motorcycle engine and also modifies an existing engine design for use with the new carburetor. Under the shrinking-back rule, the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a) are applied first at the level of the overall motorcycle engine. If the modifications to the engine when viewed as a whole (including the carburetor development) fail to satisfy the qualification requirements—for example, because less than 80% of the total activities on the overall engine constitute elements of a process of experimentation due to reliance on the existing engine design—the requirements are then applied to the next most significant subset of elements. Assuming the new carburetor is the next most significant subset of elements of the engine, the research activities involved specifically in developing the new carburetor may still constitute qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(1).

Critically, however, both the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and the Tax Court in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Dec. 23, 2024), establish that the shrinking-back rule is not self-executing. If a taxpayer tracks employee wages and supplies only at the whole-vessel, whole-building, or whole-product level (such as billing hours broadly to "Project 720 Tanker" or "HVAC"), the court cannot determine what portion of costs attached to the qualifying subcomponent (such as the tanker's stern notch or a specific hospital air-handling subsystem), resulting in complete disallowance.
Substantiation Standards and Hypothetical Worked QRE Impact Analysis
Recordkeeping Mandate (26 CFR Section 1.41-4(d)) and Oral Testimony Jurisprudence

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) (promulgated in T.D. 9104) and 26 CFR § 1.6001-1(a), a taxpayer claiming a credit under Section 41 "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit".

In Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, the Tax Court relied heavily on the credible oral testimony of ESI's Senior Vice President of Product Development, Mr. Wende, and engineering witness Mr. Hoth both to establish technical qualification across the sampled projects and to determine the nexus and percentage allocations of qualified employee services (75% for CEO Suder, 100% for SVP Wende, 100% for engineers and product managers, and 5–10% for quality control and shipping personnel) under the estimation principles of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), and United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009), even in the absence of project-specific timecards (though the court separately reduced the dollar amount of CEO Suder's $8.7 million to $11 million annual compensation eligible for QRE inclusion under the reasonable-compensation limitation of IRC § 174(e), sustaining compensation at the 90th percentile based on Mr. Longnecker's expert report while rejecting gross revenue royalties).

Conversely, subsequent judicial decisions—including Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Dec. 23, 2024)—have strictly rejected uncorroborated retrospective estimates and general witness testimony where contemporaneous documentation failed to substantiate beginning-of-project uncertainty, systematic evaluation of alternatives, investigative test protocols, and subcomponent-level labor nexus.
Hypothetical Worked Example: $1,000,000 QRE and Credit Model

First, while qualified in-house employee wages (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), covering direct conduct, direct supervision, and direct support under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)) and non-depreciable tangible supplies (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)) enter QREs at 100%, IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(1) limit general "contract research expenses" to 65 percent of any amount paid or incurred to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for qualified research performed on behalf of the taxpayer (increasing to 75% for qualified research performed by a qualified research consortium under IRC § 41(b)(3)(C), or 100% for qualified energy research performed by an eligible small business, university, or federal laboratory under IRC § 41(b)(3)(D)). Applying the mandatory 65% statutory cap to $300,000 of general third-party contractor outlays yields $195,000 ($300,000 multiplied by 0.65) in net contract research QREs, producing $895,000 in total verified QREs ($600,000 + $100,000 + $195,000) rather than $1,000,000 (to claim $300,000 in net contract QREs at the 65% rate, a taxpayer would have to incur $461,538.46 in gross contractor payments). Second, IRC § 41 does not apply a flat 10% rate; rather, taxpayers compute either the 20% Regular Credit on current-year QREs exceeding a statutory base amount (IRC § 41(a)(1) and (c), where the base amount cannot be less than 50% of current-year QREs) or the 14% Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) on current-year QREs exceeding 50% of average annual QREs for the 3 preceding taxable years (IRC § 41(c)(4)(A), or 6% if the taxpayer had no QREs in any of the 3 preceding taxable years), optionally subject to the IRC § 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election.

Hypothetical Step-by-Step Re-Computation: Assume a U.S. corporation incurs $1,000,000 in gross domestic project outlays ($600,000 in qualified W-2 wages, $100,000 in qualified testing supplies, and $300,000 paid to an unrelated U.S. engineering contractor under a prior written agreement where the taxpayer bears financial risk and retains substantial rights under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3)), elects the 14% ASC method under IRC § 41(c)(4)(A), and had $500,000 in average annual QREs over the 3 preceding taxable years, establishing a 50% ASC base amount of $250,000 ($500,000 multiplied by 0.50):

items: Step 1 (Verified Clean QREs — 0% Duplication): Sum 100% of qualified wages ($600,000) + 100% of qualified supplies ($100,000) + 65% of general contract research ($300,000 multiplied by 0.65 = $195,000) = $895,000 Total QREs. Subtract the $250,000 ASC base amount ($895,000 minus $250,000 = $645,000 Incremental QREs) and multiply by 14% ($645,000 multiplied by 0.14) = $90,300 Gross ASC Credit.

Step 2 (Shrunk-Back Subcomponent — 60% Legacy Port Excluded, 40% Novel Cloud Subcomponent Documented): Suppose 60% of project outlays across each cost category went to routine COBOL-to-Java code translation and interface reverse engineering (excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B)–(C)), disqualifying the overall software release under the 80% substantially-all rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), but the taxpayer maintained granular subcomponent timecards and commit logs isolating the remaining 40% spent on a novel, technically uncertain distributed caching subcomponent under the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2). Qualifying subcomponent costs equal 40% of wages ($240,000) + 40% of supplies ($40,000) + 65% of the 40% contractor spend ($120,000 multiplied by 0.65 = $78,000) = $358,000 Total QREs. Subtracting the fixed $250,000 ASC base amount leaves $108,000 Incremental QREs ($358,000 minus $250,000), yielding a 14% ASC credit of $15,120 ($108,000 multiplied by 0.14).

Step 3 (Unrebutted Duplication — Exceeds 20% Duplication with No Subcomponent Logs): If the same 60% duplicative/routine port is commingled with the 40% experimental work in a single whole-project bucket without subcomponent time tracking (the Little Sandy Coal and Phoenix Design Group trap), the overall business component fails the 80% substantially-all test (40% is less than 80%), shrinking-back cannot be applied for lack of subcomponent cost records, and qualified QREs drop to $0, forfeiting the entire $90,300 credit.

Interaction with IRC Section 174 and Section 174A Cost Recovery and Pre-Filing Compliance Protocols
The Section 174 and Section 174A Classification Tension

Because IRC § 41 applies only to a subset of the research expenditures governed by the Code's R&E cost-recovery provisions, distinguishing non-duplicated experimental development from routine duplication carries major tax-accounting consequences for deduction timing as well as tax credits.

Under Section 13206(a) and (e) of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97, Dec. 22, 2017, 131 Stat. 2111), for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, taxpayers were prohibited from currently deducting "specified research or experimental expenditures" (including software development under IRC § 174(c)(3)) and were instead required to charge such expenditures to capital account and amortize them ratably over a 5-year period for domestic research and a 15-year period for foreign research (within the meaning of IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)), beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which such expenditures were paid or incurred.

Subsequently, on July 4, 2025, Congress enacted the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21, title VII, § 70302, 139 Stat. 191), implemented administratively by IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (effective August 28, 2025). First, OBBBA § 70302(a) added new IRC § 174A ("Domestic research or experimental expenditures"), which permanently restores a 100% current deduction under IRC § 174A(a) for domestic R&E expenditures (including software development under IRC § 174A(d)(3)) paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, while permitting taxpayers under IRC § 174A(c)(1) to elect to capitalize and amortize domestic R&E expenditures over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month the taxpayer first realizes benefits. Second, OBBBA § 70302(f)(1) allows eligible small businesses (taxpayers other than tax shelters meeting the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test—$25 million, inflation-adjusted to $31 million for 2025) to elect to apply IRC § 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, while OBBBA § 70302(f)(2) allows all taxpayers to elect to deduct remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E balances either in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over a 2-taxable-year period. Third, OBBBA § 70302(b)(1) amended IRC § 174 so that for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, Section 174 applies exclusively to foreign research or experimental expenditures, which remain subject to mandatory 15-year midpoint amortization under IRC § 174(a)(2)(B) and strict non-deductibility upon property disposition, retirement, or abandonment after May 12, 2025 under IRC § 174(d). Fourth, OBBBA § 70302(b)(2)(B) amended IRC § 280C(c)(1) so that domestic R&E expenditures deducted or capitalized under IRC § 174A must be reduced by the amount of the gross Section 41(a) research credit unless the taxpayer timely elects the reduced credit under IRC § 280C(c)(2).

For open pre-2025 taxable years (2022–2024) where a taxpayer does not qualify for or elect retroactive small-business expensing under OBBBA § 70302(f)(1), as well as in states that decouple from IRC § 174A and retain mandatory 5-year domestic amortization (such as Maryland), claiming the Section 41 credit requires treating the underlying domestic costs as specified R&E expenditures subject to 5-year capitalization rather than ordinary deductible business expenses. Conversely, for post-2024 taxable years under IRC § 174A (and for offshore engineering activities where taxpayers must distinguish foreign R&E subject to 15-year amortization under amended IRC § 174 from routine non-R&E production or duplication), genuine blueprint duplication, routine code translation, or build-to-print fabrication is not research in the "experimental or laboratory sense" under 26 CFR § 1.174-2; such routine duplication falls instead under ordinary business expense or cost-of-goods-sold rules and cannot support a Section 41 tax credit.
Actionable Pre-Filing Protocols for Form 6765 and Audit Defense

items: Conduct a Pre-Filing Input and "Delta" Risk Assessment: Before populating Form 6765 Section G and Section F, audit the starting informational inputs of every claimed business component—specifically customer CAD drawings, OEM specifications, legacy codebases, published industry standards, and physical competitor samples—and define the exact technical "delta" (such as isolating a novel ceramic bearing subcomponent or a new multi-zone cooling process in Column 49(d) under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)), stripping all teardown, dimensional measurement, and replication hours out of Columns 50–56 so they neither dilute the 80% substantially-all threshold nor violate the 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) residual exclusion rule.

Enforce Problem Statements and Alternative Evaluation Logs: Require every R&D project charter to open with a dated technical problem statement specifying why existing public standards, building codes, or commercial off-the-shelf designs fail to establish the capability, method, or appropriate design (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)), paired with a contemporaneous alternatives log documenting the competing engineering designs modeled, simulated, or tested and rejected (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i)).

Apply Proactive Subcomponent Shrinking-Back (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)): Rather than claiming an overall "me-too" commercial product, full hospital MEPF system, or entire marine vessel on an all-or-nothing basis—the fatal litigation error in Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287) and Phoenix Design Group (T.C. Memo. 2024-113)—configure project timekeeping codes and Form 6765 Section G line items at the sub-assembly, specialized algorithm, or manufacturing-process level from project inception.

Preserve Negative Knowledge and Independent Expert Validation: Retain physical, photographic, or digital records of failed prototypes, rejected FEA/CFD simulation iterations, bug logs, and scrapped test batches (which prove genuine experimental risk where blueprint copying would succeed linearly), and for high-scrutiny claims—such as large software architecture refactors or generic pharmaceutical synthesis processes—obtain contemporaneous technical memoranda from qualified subject-matter experts documenting why the method or design was uncertain at project start.

Screen Contracts Separately for Blueprint Duplication (§ 41(d)(4)(C)) and Funded Research (§ 41(d)(4)(H)): Review Master Service Agreements, Statements of Work, and purchase orders along two independent legal axes: first, verifying whether client documents specify functional performance goals rather than detailed design blueprints (IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4)), and second, verifying that payment contingency risk and substantial intellectual-property rights reside with the claimant (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(3), (e)(2)–(3), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)).
